title: The Pull You Can't See
question: What makes a magnet pull on some things but not others?
hook: Every substance is a little magnetic, yet only a few metals ever stick to your fridge.
idea: Magnetism comes from electric currents and particle moments, and only a few materials show it strongly enough to feel.

beats.prompt: You hold a strong magnet next to a copper pipe and a steel nail. Only the nail clings. What is going on with the copper?

choices.label: Copper has no magnetism of any kind
choices.feedback: Tempting, but every substance shows some magnetism; copper is just weakly repelled.

choices.label: Copper is weakly repelled, too faintly to feel
Copper is strongly attracted but too heavy to move
choices.feedback: Copper is not strongly attracted; its response is weak, not blocked by weight.

beats.explain: All substances exhibit some magnetism. Copper is diamagnetic, so the push is real but usually only lab instruments can detect it.

beats.prompt: match each material to how it responds to a magnetic field
pairs: Strongly attracted, can become a magnet
beats.explain: Ferromagnetic, paramagnetic, diamagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials each answer a field differently.

beats.prompt: put these discoveries in the order they happened
items: Ancient people notice lodestones attract iron
Gilbert concludes the Earth is a magnet
Oersted sees a current move a compass
Faraday induces a voltage with a changing flux
beats.explain: Lodestones came first, then Gilbert in 1600, Oersted in 1820 and Faraday in 1831.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Iron, cobalt and nickel are strongly attracted to magnets.
Most everyday objects are not pulled by a magnet.
So most everyday objects have no magnetism at all.
Their response exists but is usually only detectable with lab instruments.
beats.explain: All substances exhibit some magnetism; the weak types are just too faint to feel, so we call them non-magnetic.
